newsitem.title: USA: Dole says Clinton administration is unethical.
newsitem.headline: Dole says Clinton administration is unethical.

text.p: Republican presidential challenger Bob Dole stepped up his attacks on President Bill Clinton on Monday charging he has an unethical administration, and promised to get tougher in their final, crucial debate on Wednesday.

At a rally en route from Washington to San Diego for the debate, Dole asked about 1,000 supporters in downtown Kansas City if they thought he was too easy on Clinton their first time out, on Oct. 6. When the crowd responded in the affirmative, Dole said, "I thought so too."

Dole, apparently listening to advisers urging him to hit the character issue harder, said about 30 members of Clinton's administration "are already gone -- they are in jail or they are indicted or they are out of there."
"Then he talks about an ethical administration. Well he does not have an ethical administration and we're going to go after him on that on Wednesday night," he added.

Dole recalled the late Democratic President Harry Truman, from nearby Independence, Missouri, used to say, "The buck stops here," but he added his own twist: "Bill Clinton says the buck doesn't stop anywhere. It just keeps on going."

Separately, Dole press secretary Nelson Warfield criticised some contributions of $425,000 to the Democratic Party from people with ties to an Indonesian banking group and a $250,000 foreign contribution to Democrats from a South Korean group, which was returned as it violated campaign laws.
"This is the latest chapter in a story of scandals that has plagued this administration," Warfield told reporters. "You have to wonder if at some point the public will say enough is enough."

At the rally, Dole again hit at the "trustworthy" issue, saying that Clinton promised a middle income tax cut in Kansas four years ago and has not delivered. He used the trust line to say he would deliver on his own promise of a 15 percent across-the-board income tax rate cut.

"It's your money, it's your money, it's your money," Dole said, repeating his stump mantra of recent weeks. When Clinton backers in the crowd heckled him, Dole said they too would get the tax cuts when Clinton is out of office.

But Dole is running far behind in this key midwestern state with 11 electoral votes. A St. Louis Post Dispatch poll on Sunday showed the trouble he is having in a state where Clinton easily defeated President George Bush four years ago. Clinton leads by 19 percentage points, 53 to 34 percent. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot trails with 4 percent.

Dole's main task this week is to deliver a powerful, winning performance in the Wednesday debate at the University of San Diego. After their first debate on Oct. 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, polls said people were impressed with Dole's performance and wit but still a majority said Clinton won.

Some of Dole's aides have been pressing him to get tougher on the so-called character issue, which the former senator has been hitting with glancing blows on the campaign trail, arguing chiefly that character counts and voters cannot trust Clinton to keep his promises.
Dole plans to spend his time in San Diego before the debate preparing for the encounter, although he has a hotel luncheon speech scheduled on Tuesday before the Electronic Industries Association.
